description: We are a passionate team of students and tech enthusiasts participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We combine programming, AI, design, storytelling, and problem-solving to turn real-world challenges into engaging experiences. This year, we are building an interactive educational game that makes science fun, meaningful, and accessible.
summary: Lunar Outpost: Survival Equation is a browser-based isometric survival game that teaches kids aged 7-12 the real science of lunar exploration. Players command a damaged moon base and balance power, water, and oxygen while facing solar storms, extreme heat, and the 14-day lunar night. Every decision is a two-option trade-off, built on one principle: no choice is free. Wrong choices cause realistic damage, and the game explains the cause and the best solution. Across three levels, players repair sensors, forecast solar events with a telescope, and expand the base. The game uses NASA’s DONKI, OSDR, and Artemis lunar surface data, and it runs instantly on any device with no installation.
details:
Project Details (English, for the NASA portal field)

What it does and how it works
Lunar Outpost: Survival Equation is a browser-based isometric survival simulator that teaches children aged 7-12 the real science behind living on the Moon. The player commands a damaged lunar base and keeps power, water, and oxygen balanced while facing solar radiation storms, extreme daytime heat, and the 14-day lunar night. Every crisis is a quick two-option decision built on one engineering principle: no choice is free.

The game has three levels:

  • Level 1, Emergency & Survival: Repair the environmental sensor array and stabilize core resources. The solar telescope is locked, so radiation storms arrive unpredictably.
  • Level 2, Forecasting & Adaptation: The battery-powered telescope unlocks. Players observe sunspots and incoming meteors to anticipate radiation events and respond in time.
  • Level 3, Base Expansion & Mission Completion: Players upgrade base modules, earn a Hint Key, and return safely to Earth for a final performance evaluation.

Solving tasks earns Wrench & Bolts currency for repairs and upgrades. Unresolved malfunctions reduce efficiency: one causes a minor loss, two trigger a critical alert, and three drop the base to 50%. Wrong choices cause realistic damage, and the game explains the cause, the effect, and the best solution. Difficult terms have built-in kid-friendly definitions.

How NASA data supports it

  • DONKI: Shapes solar flare timing, sunspot activity, and coronal mass ejection events.
  • OSDR: Calibrates radiation exposure effects on the crew and shielding requirements.
  • Artemis & lunar surface data: Governs the 14-day day/night cycle, temperature extremes, and landing-site terrain.

The data is stored as structured JSON profiles that drive events, resource drain, and consequences.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Makes lunar engineering understandable and fun for children without heavy reading.
  • Teaches cause and effect, resource management, and decision-making under constraints.
  • Runs instantly on any device with a browser and needs no installation, so it is easy to use in schools and at home.
  • Intended impact: inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers by showing that real space missions are built on trade-offs.

Tools, languages, and software

  • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript for the web application
  • JSON for structured scientific data profiles
  • Deployed as a live web app, playable on any modern browser [add hosting platform]
  • Manus AI as a development assistant for code generation, kid-friendly glossary text, isometric sprites, and audio cues. All generated content is disclosed in the project metadata and description.
  • Hardware: no special hardware required.

How the project is creative

  • It turns real NASA datasets into game mechanics, so each gameplay moment (a storm, a heat wave, the long night) comes from actual space science.
  • The "no choice is free" rule makes trade-offs the core of the game, instead of simple right-or-wrong quizzes.
  • Wrong choices become learning moments, because the game explains exactly what went wrong and why.
  • The fair-play Hint system (one use, minus 3 points, confirmation warning) keeps the educational assessment honest.

Factors the team considered

  • Age range: The game had to work for both 7-year-olds and 12-year-olds, so we used high-contrast icons, color-coded gauges, guided onboarding, and minimal text.
  • Scientific accuracy vs. simplicity: We kept the NASA-based events and trade-offs authentic but simplified the values for children.
  • Accessibility: A zero-installation web app works across devices, including low-cost ones.
  • Responsible use of SI: The team conceived the idea, structure, and data mapping. Manus AI supported implementation only, all generated content is disclosed, and no NASA branding was used or modified.
